endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: To validate that training is achieving its intended goals, HDOs should implement a tiered competency validation approach calibrated to the risk level and workflow impact of each AI solution.

endorsements.title: Stakeholder-centric participation in large language models enhanced health systems
endorsements.quote: By offering tailored learning modules specific to different roles and simulating healthcare scenarios, LLMs can facilitate hands-on practice that deepens understanding and builds confidence 63 .

endorsements.title: The Ethical Boundaries of Chairside Generative Artificial Intelligence in Dental Education
endorsements.quote: Students and faculty should receive training on AI ethics and limitations before applying this knowledge in the clinic.

endorsements.title: Collaborative and Cooperative Hospital "In-House" Medical Device Development and Implementation in the AI Age: The European Responsible AI Development (EURAID) Framework Compatible With European Values
endorsements.quote: In order to build AI literacy among HCP in a safe and controlled environment, training methods such as simulation-based modules [ 125 , 126 ] (ie, practice in realistic settings [ 125 , 127 ]), case-based exercises [ 128 ], and interactive workshops [ 129 ] can help to explore tools repeatedly without risking patient safety while facilitating experimental learning.

endorsements.title: Navigating the artificial intelligence landscape in trauma, critical care and emergency general surgery: insights from the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) 2025 Annual Meeting Panel Discussion
endorsements.quote: Simulation was additionally highlighted as a practical setting for rehearsing workflows that incorporate AI and for practicing “no-tech” scenarios when systems fail or are unavailable.

endorsements.title: Bridging the Implementation Gap in Medical AI Education: 3-Lever Framework for Concurrent Reform
endorsements.quote: We suggest that faculties invest in secure digital “sandboxes” and simulated EHRs that embed AI decision support tools.

endorsements.title: AI and System Evolution in CPD: Integrating CHAT with a Unified Theory of Emergent System Evolution
endorsements.issuer: The Journal of continuing education in the health professions
endorsements.quote: Simulation is valuable for practicing responses to AI errors.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence in Psychiatric Graduate Medical Education
endorsements.issuer: Academic psychiatry : the journal of the American Association of Directors of Psychiatric Residency Training and the Association for Academic Psychiatry
endorsements.quote: Adopt an incremental access model for AI documentation tools, progressing from restricted use during PGY1–2 when documentation skills are still being acquired to Academic Psychiatry graduated access as trainees demonstrate competency in accurate clinical documentation and case formulation, thereby preventing un-skilling or mis-skilling while optimizing efficiency.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether sandbox, simulation, or shadowing training before live use reduces early-use AI errors, and no study documents how often such errors occur. Seven sources endorse the practice, and all but one are commentaries.

perspectives.view: The support consists of one governance framework (CHAI) and six commentaries, and none of them report outcome data. No trial, cohort, or before-and-after study compares pre-deployment simulation training with on-the-job learning. Under GRADE conventions, expert endorsement cannot substitute for a test of the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The targeted failure mode is plausible, since staff new to a tool may misread or over-trust its outputs. No study here measures the frequency or severity of early-use errors on live patients. Two commentaries propose simulation for rehearsing AI errors and system outages, but no study shows that this rehearsal catches errors before they reach patients.

CHAI proposes tiered competency validation matched to each tool's risk and workflow impact, and one commentary suggests simulated EHRs with embedded AI decision support. No study reports how much staff time these environments require, how faithfully they mirror production systems, or whether skills transfer to live workflows.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems need studies that compare simulation- or sandbox-trained staff with staff trained on live patients after the same AI tool deployment. These studies should measure early-use error rates, override and acceptance patterns, time to competency, and patient harm. A baseline study that documents how often early-use AI errors occur would also show whether the hazard is large enough to justify the training cost.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell whether simulation scenarios that omit interpreter use, low-literacy communication, or the resource limits of safety-net settings would prepare staff for AI-supported care of those patients.
